utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The parties have received our message yesterday evening, I take it, where one of the messages said that you are instructed to finish this morning, you are urged to do so, of course, we never can forecast what will happen. I instructed VWS to have the next witness to see at approximately midday whether the next witness should remain on standby or whether we'll start. Let's try to be as efficient as possible. Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were discussing yesterday the methodology of your approach, and we'd, I think, reached the point where we were dealing with the difference in approaches to the reports. If I can pick up where we left off there, I was asking you about what it was that had led you to take this different approach in the Milosevic case and in this case, and perhaps I should remind you of where -- of your final answer. I don't know if you you remember it. I think yesterday you said in response to my question what was the approach made in the first instance in the Milosevic case, and you said: "Well that actually came out of some discussions that I had when I was preparing the report for the Krajisnik case. I had requested Assembly sessions going into the summer and fall of 1992 which I had not previously seen. I requested those of the Prosecution and perceived that this was an extraordinary source which illuminated more than just a few months prior to the beginning of the conflict." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you like to elaborate further?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to say that in reviewing those transcripts and then returning to the Krajisnik team who had commissioned the report I was working on for them, that I -- those sessions were at that point not translated. They were only in Serbian. And so I expressed to them an interest in actually using those for extending the time-line of my Krajisnik report into the summer, and they asked me not to do that, but at the same time they became aware that I found the reports are of -- or the transcripts to be an extraordinary source, and so when I was first contacted by the Milosevic team, they then asked me to consider using the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions for a report much like the one that's in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But a big shift from taking this approach which relied upon a number of sources in your earlier report to then abandoning, it seems, those sources and just relying upon the one source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I don't see it as a major shift. I think, first of all, you should recognise that the sources being cited in the Bosnian Serb Assembly are in fact probably 50 or 60 different sources. They are the various individuals who made speeches in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And those sources are extremely good quality sources by virtue of who they were, what they knew, and the fact that they were speaking under conditions that they assumed to be confidential. So I see the -- this as simply another way of presenting a narrative into the various categories which effectively each answers a question that one would pose of the sources, their answers already being of course on record. So I see the -- I view the excerpts report as a series of narratives that I would certainly grant require the reader to concentrate more and to in fact comprehend the connective tissue that links them together in a narrative, but nevertheless, a very similar approach to the other reports that I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I please have on e-court 1D01205. This is the report prepared by you, Mr. Donia, in the Krajisnik case. Now, if we could go over the page to page -- it's the first page of the report itself after the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we look at the second paragraph there, and the approach you took in the Krajisnik case --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name is Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Krajisnik, thank you. "Source citations are provided so the reader can assess the authenticity and credibility of the information provided. Studies based in part upon the transcripts and minutes of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and other documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Other sources include the contemporary periodical press, scholarly studies, published document collections, published and broadcast memoirs of participants and observers, and other materials in the public domain." Is it your evidence that that approach is similar to the approach you took in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough, if that's what you assert. Did you -- at what stage did you cross-reference the, let me call it the Stanisic report with these types of materials, contemporaneous periodical press, scholarly studies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not in the report itself, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, at what stage did you yourself do it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I treated my knowledge derived from those sources as background, but did not cite such sources in the Stanisic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's forget about citing them in the Stanisic report, at what stage did you sit down with the excerpts, the Stanisic report, and go through it in your own time cross-referencing to these what must have been hundreds of other sources? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I use a master chronology file which is voluminous and draws upon a whole host of sources which provides me with a kind of a framework within which to view any new material that I look at or any source material that may require being situated in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So let me understand this. When you put together the excerpts, were you then following this process by which you used your master chronology file, or did you compile the excerpts and then later on sit down and check it once you'd finished the report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's back and forth. I use the chronology file as a resource. If I encounter a particular session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, I go to that file to see what else was going on. If there's a reference in that session to a prior event, I always go to that file to see if it corresponds to what's being reported in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. So it's an interactive process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So in short, you did it while you were compiling the excerpts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And yet didn't then include that checking into and put it into footnotes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I -- I, you know, had no intention of producing a three-volume study which is what happens when you start to lard up a fairly simple source report like this with extraneous citations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the Chamber wonder, the point you are making is clear now, was clear yesterday already. I think we also told you more or less that we understood that the lack of transparency in other sources used is perfectly clear, and the Chamber wonders why we do not go to the substance of -- unless there's any specific issue that you wanted to raise, but we are going around source materials again and we've done that for quite some time by now so that point is perfectly clear. Whatever may explain the choice of doing it this way, but unless there's one specific point, and then please address that as soon as possible, otherwise go to the subject matter of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I will, if I may, just continue on this subject but take Your Honours to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I suggest that the reason that you didn't take this -- the approach you've taken with other cases other than Milosevic was that in fact you considered, along with the Prosecution, that this was the best way of supporting the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the case. I think the excerpts themselves will tell you that the purpose of this particular report was to shed light on a lot of different events, attitudes, some of which in fact go in directions quite apart from what the Prosecution might argue in some instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The approach you took was to -- what was the question then you were seeking to address? You were looking at what was relevant to the indictment, is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, in this particular report to enlighten or provide some answers to the questions that correspond to the eight categories or topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who gave you the eight categories or topics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I selected those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: After being asked to find excerpts which were relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the first step was find excerpts relevant to the indictment. Did you sit down with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as a response to that, you then said, well, the approach I'm going to take is to categorise my task into these eight titles, this will best achieve what I've been asked to do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my approach I guess wasn't quite that lawyerly. It was rather to look at the outcome of what I had done for the Milosevic report and see in that report that I probably had not systematised the material, to my satisfaction anyway, topically, so I reviewed that. I reviewed actually the testimony and the cross-examination under Mr. Milosevic and concluded that would be much more useful to the Court to have something that was topically organised within the broad questions or issues that arise in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't think it would be beneficial to build on the report or to do a similar report to the report on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that report was available, could have been submitted by anybody at any time in the case, so I didn't see any value in trying to let's say create some sort of hybrid of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go please to page 12 of this report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a bit about some of the views you put forward in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 12 which is ERN 02910921, the English. I think it is in English. That's 13, I think. Sorry, could we go to the next page, that's 11. We've gone to 10 I think now. It's a bit confusing because it's in reverse order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just second paragraph there, just very quickly, the sentence: "Babic, on the other hand, accepted Milosevic as an authentic spokesman. 'Serbs in Croatia have always believed that Milosevic is a true representative of the Serbian people, said Babic, and he will not betray the interests of any part of the Serbian people in Yugoslavia.'" Is that a view you still adhere to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a statement of Babic's view at the time, and my understanding of Babic's view at that time remains the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I am interested where -- the first paragraph, at its first session, on 3rd of -- I am sorry to take this out of any sort of structure, but I want to be as quick as I can in dealing with this evidence. "At its first session on the 31st of July, 1990, the SNV Knin authorised a plebiscite of the Serbian people on the question of autonomy from Croatia. Before the plebiscite was scheduled to begin, Croatian police attempted on 17th of August to secure control of police stations in several Serb-majority towns. A staff for city defence in Knin headed by Babic proclaimed a war situation and barricades were erected on roads leading into several towns." Do you adhere to that view, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, that -- I'm citing Radulovic's Serbian Krajina there, that's certainly what that book told me, and he was a reporter from a Serbian newspaper, so I accepted that. I frankly don't know whether any other information may have surfaced since then to nuance that understanding of the situation or not. It certainly could be the case. I haven't followed it, but I would hold to Radulovic's description as of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 14, please, and the paragraph I'm interested in is the second full paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Even as the Croatian state was acquiring arms from Hungary and other countries, Serbian separatists were acquiring the means to contest Croatian authority in several areas of the republic. Beginning in spring 1991, JNA officers distributed thousands of weapons to SDS members and others who supported Serbian separatism. Croatian Serbs received various infantry weapons, anti-aircraft guns, mortars, and ammunition from the JNA armouries. By the beginning of June, one JNA officer reported 15.000 weapons had been transferred." Again, do you still adhere to that view?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know we are very concerned with methodology here, so I would like to see the footnote, if I can, to that number 64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Footnote 64 reads: "Colonel Dusan Smiljanic to General Ratko Mladic, Knin, 15th of October, 1994," and then it gives the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would hold that that was the statement made in that document by Colonel Smiljanovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I meant the -- I go further than that. Did you put this into the report because you accepted there was cogent evidence that this was correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put it into the report, the entire paragraph, because I believed I had cogent evidence that that was the case, including the Croatian state acquiring arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go over the page, please, to page 15. The paragraph I'm interested in is the last full paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Not long after armed conflict ended in Slovenia, skirmishes in Croatia escalated into full war. Kijevo, a Croat village on the road connecting Knin and Split was surrounded by rural Serbian settlements. In spring 1991, Croats from Kijevo erected barricades to prevent Serbian intrusions into their village. In August 1991, Serbs from the nearby villages appealed to the Knin Corps of the JNA to remove the barriers and to give them weapons. The newly appointed deputy corps's commander, Ratko Mladic, soon obliged them. In co-operation with Milan Martic, the minister of the interior of SAO Knin, Mladic's JNA artillery bombed the village on 28th of August, 1991." I'll just stop there and ask do you still adhere to that view? Was there cogent evidence of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had cogent evidence at the time in the form of the source that I've cited at that point, and I believe that that source was an excellent one and on that basis put it in there. I -- as I say, there may be other things that have taken place in the meantime that would nuance or slightly change that account of events if I were aware of them, but I have not followed that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on: "In co-operation with Milan Martic, the minister the interior of SAO Knin, Mladic's JNA artillery bombed the village on 28th of August, 1991. Kijevo, characterised by Croats as the Croatian Alamo, was conquered by Martic's police in short order. Local Serb forces killed some Croats and drove others from the village. Martic later recalled, it was a joint action between the army and in two days we liberated Kijevo. The army provided the heavy weapons and I provided the infantry." Same question, do you still adhere to that view?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adhere to the quote that was provided in the Silber and Little book and do not know of what may have come to light in the meantime to slightly change or alter the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I intervened is that when you start reading, speed goes up immediately and the translators are not able to follow. So when I stop you, it is because I'm checking whether the other languages can still follow your speed of speech. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll slow down. Can we go to page 30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We move now to the title "The Transformation of the JNA in BH." "The formation and conduct of military and paramilitary organisations in BH took place in the long shadow of the war in Croatia. By early 1992, each of the three nationalist parties in BH had taken measures to prepare militarily for war and were able to call upon paramilitary organisations to support their aims. But the decisive role in the militarisation of BH was played by two socialist era military organisations: The local Territorial Defence forces and the JNA." Is that a view you adhere to today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you would not mind, what exercise are you in at this moment? Do you want to add to the evidence of the witness by taking parts of his other reports in order to have them in evidence or are you in ten minutes from now starting asking nasty questions about what you consider perhaps not to be correct? What is the exercise we are in at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The exercise is one, to add to the witness's evidence, and two, to demonstrate that there is a reason why this witness didn't take the same approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But now, as far as the first part of the exercise is concerned, have you asked Mr. Groome whether he would be willing to agree with page that and that, so and so, so that you would agree with on that. I don't know whether this has been done, because we now go through all of this where it's all on paper, the only question is is this what your opinion still is. If that's the case, these opinions represented in other cases by the Prosecution. So I wondered whether we could not have found a more effective, more efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I accept full responsibility for that. I should have spoken to Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution wouldn't object to the entire report being admitted into evidence in -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I can imagine that -- I don't know whether you have any problems with other parts of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't want the whole report. It's only the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that makes it clear that you should have asked Mr. Groome and say, well, we have a report with limited sources, we have broader reports from other cases, I'd like to introduce as agreed upon or as in evidence those and those parts of the report, would you have any problem with that, and then we would have saved half an hour, perhaps. I don't know how long you will continue, but let's try to get to the core. You want additional evidence, Mr. Groome apparently doesn't oppose to any of it. You could even stop now and say during the next break to Mr. Groome, those, those, those parts. That's what I want. And at the same time, of course, it is clear that the evidence you are now taking from the other reports is -- well, is at least to some extent sourced, sometimes just a book or just a newspaper, how reliable that is, apparently as Mr. Donia told us, he considers the sources excellent, or at least I take it that you considered them reliable enough to -- not to put any question marks to the findings. It's also clear that whatever you add now was not clearly included in the previous report and that you apparently take the view that therefore the present report gives an incomplete picture of what is relevant for this case. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, I would just be concerned about context and taking things out of context, but I would give my prior agreement to accept any paragraph taken in its entirety from this report, this way the Chamber at least has the benefit of the entire thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you please proceed on the basis of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- mutual understanding of how we could use the knowledge and the skills of Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please on the screen, D305. Yes, I beg your pardon, I've given you the wrong citation. It's 1D01201. Apologies. 1D01201. It was D305 in the Karadzic case, that's the error I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If you just read it and just familiarise yourself with it again and just assist the Chamber with what this is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a open letter that a substantial number of people, including myself, signed appealing to the ICTY to release all the evidence in the minutes and transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to shortcut this as much as possible, but if everyone has had a chance to read the first page, can we go to the second page. When was this letter sent approximately?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. It was three or four years ago, something like that. It says one year after the ICJ decision, and I can't even recall exactly when that was, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this letter was sent before or, well, I presume it was sent before you wrote the report in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the second paragraph reads: "However, the ICJ is not the only United Nations court that failed to uphold the principles of international law. The ICTY judges granted Serbia's request that the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council be submitted in a censored version, allegedly because Serbia's national security was at stake. This would be equivalent to the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg agreeing to withhold key evidence against the Nazi leaders out of respect for Germany's national security. The ICTY's concession to Serbia was the result of a political agreement reached by the Tribunal with the Serbian government, and is therefore evidence again that the international courts have allowed politics to interfere with the legal process." Presumably that was your view because you signed the letter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was your view then that the ICTY, the judges at least that made this decision, were being politically influenced?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were making a political decision, I would say. I don't know that they were being politically influenced by any particular group, but I think that the language there speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, politically influenced by the Serbian government, that's the way I would read the language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they cited -- they accepted the Serbian argument that national security was at stake, and that was a political agreement, and the letter goes on to state that this is evidence that the international courts have allowed politics to interfere with the legal process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. So this is a mindset which you had when you approached your task of compiling the reports for testifying in -- at the ICTY, is that not logical?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a pretty minor consideration that arose in the context of the ICJ case, and I wouldn't say it was an important part of my mind set as I approached the testimony before this -- before the various Chambers of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, as you approached the selection of the excerpts in this report, presumably that was somewhere in your mind as you sought to demonstrate what was relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it was about the farthest thing from my mind. The selection, its processes sufficiently challenging and complex to be completely consuming without this kind of consideration going into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Pretty strong comparison to compare the Serbs to the Nazis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the basic point is correct that indeed, at least from what I have seen of SDC minutes, that this was not in fact a matter of Serbia's national security but of individual Serbs within the Serb government that were being protected, so I would stand by the basic view here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Comparison. You would stand by the basic comparison?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would stand by the basic view that I've expressed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Then further down, the next paragraph: "As representatives of the academic community human rights activists and intellectuals from all over the word, we demand that the international public be told the whole truth. We therefore request that the full and uncensored minutes of the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council be made public so that the role of the Serbian state in the genocide in Bosnia and Herzegovina can be assessed objectively." That paragraph appears to assume a conclusion which is that there was a genocide in the Serbian -- sorry in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is that -- was that a view that you adhered to when approaching the compilation of this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it really wasn't a -- it was a view that I adhered to at the time that I was preparing this report. Certainly had been ruled a genocide by this -- Chambers of this Tribunal and by the ICJ, so it was a view I adhered to. It wasn't -- again it wasn't part of my mindset when I went about compiling the excerpts for the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, this letter was, and we can go, I think, up the page from where we've just read, this letter was pointing out, wasn't it, or expressing a view that the genocide which had been found at Srebrenica was in fact too limited a view and in fact what you were urging was the acceptance of genocide across the whole of Bosnia by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to look at the specific language because I don't recall that portion of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go up the page, please, to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There it is, the first paragraph is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're -- it misrepresented what this actually says because the letter does indeed call into question the notion that genocide occurred nowhere except Srebrenica, but does not conclude or allege that it occurred elsewhere. It merely cites the calling into question in two of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm just reading that paragraph where it questioned whether genocide -- let me start that again. I mean, I'm reading that paragraph in conjunction with the paragraph below where there seems to be in the writers' minds or the signatories' minds an approach to genocide at the ICJ which is wrong, and then down the page the paragraph would appear to suggest that what the international court should be doing is finding genocide in other places. If that's not your intention and I'm putting an erroneous interpretation, then feel free to say.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- again, I can't see this whole document one piece at a time, and I can't really put together what you are citing, but that was not my, let's say, intent at the time, and I don't believe that it is what the letter actually states. You may have an interpretation of it that is that way, but it wasn't -- that wasn't one that I shared at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, did you approach the putting together of these excerpts with the mindset that the international courts had failed to recognise the genocide elsewhere other than Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you hold that view?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly true that the international courts have not recognised genocide outside of Srebrenica. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, that's not the question. The question is do you hold the view that that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you another question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question as to whether it's wrong or not, I don't know. I frankly go back and forth in my own mind about that issue and really don't have a definitive opinion of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, you do think it and sometimes no, you don't think it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I think there's a very good case for it and other times I, you know, and this is usually in the course of reviewing evidence, and I look at the extent to which various panels at this Tribunal have wrestled with that issue very -- obviously very conscientiously and can see the reasons that they would conclude that there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the report, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, may I tender this as an exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have some more water, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask that some more water be provided to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We go please to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask you one question, Mr. Donia. Are you familiar with the kind of decisions a court takes halfway in this Tribunal? That is, a decision on a motion that there's no case to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there is at least in this statement quite some speculation as to what would have been the outcome of the case and that you compared the outcome of the ICJ decision with a halfway decision, as we call it, 98 bis, and that there is quite some speculation as to what would have been the case if the ICJ would have had available these reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Yes, I agree. I think it's a matter of mere speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But nevertheless, there's no hesitation to call it a miscarriage of justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the miscarriage of justice I'm referring to is the failure to consult the SDC minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that if there is a procedural flaw that you do not hesitate to call it a miscarriage of justice because that's -- you are pointing at a procedural step in your view that should have been taken and if it's not taken, you always understood the miscarriage of justice that the whole of the judgement is a mistake, is incorrect, is so basically affected that it's not just a matter of speculation whether the outcome is right or wrong, but that is a strong suspicion that this procedural flaw must have had as a consequences that the outcome is not reliable anymore? That's my understanding. I'm just trying to understand your language and for that purpose I give you my understanding of what a miscarriage of justice might come down to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly take your point, Your Honour. And I think the term "miscarriage of justice" here was not intended or was not used in the sense that you have just used it. I think it was used perhaps loosely and without alleging that the -- intending to allege that the entire judgement was a miscarriage. Now, I have to say that I didn't draft this letter up. I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But may I understand this to be that you might not have been very cautious or very diligent in reviewing the language used here and that it's more an overall impression which bothered you which led to this signing this letter, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the case. I do have strong feelings about the SDC minutes but for reasons that are somewhat apart from some of the considerations here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree with me that if you sign specifically as an academic, that more diligence could have been expected? I mean, if you are a politician, I don't expect you to do anything else than to give the one-liners you find most suitable to your cause, but here I think as a matter of fact, it's specifically -- I take it at least that you signed it as an academic and not as an activist or -- I mean, we have several categories here of people who signed this document and activist, of course, I would say, are to some extent similar to politicians in their approach of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The answer is yes. And I have -- I think this is probably the last letter. I've been asked to sign dozens of letters since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I just -- I don't. I have not. I might sign one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but your point is something I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do you regret that you signed this as an academic, although you may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I would concur that I think the terminology here is a little bit loose and better caution should have been exercised. I should have exercised more caution in reviewing it and the use of the specific language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One final question. This is about the decision of the ICJ, and it says in the first paragraph that it was a betrayal of the principle that international criminal law should act to prevent, is the ICJ exercising any criminal jurisdiction in your view or how do I have to understand that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I don't know. I don't believe it is, but I'm not absolutely certain that it isn't exercising some criminal jurisdiction with that decision on genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just picking up on the issue of your view concerning genocide, did you attend the 7th biannual meeting of the international association of genocide scholars in 2007 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I did. I think I was invited to that meeting and probably appeared on the programme, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: One second. You were invited and you were there invited to be the chair in a discussion on the geography of genocide against Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited. I recall being on the programme, seeing the programme and being surprised to see that my name was there because I did not accept the invitation. It was a, you know, fully paid trip to Sarajevo. I did not feel comfortable accepting that kind of compensation from the programme organisers and didn't feel comfortable actually being a part of the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you attended or been invited to attend any other such programmes in the last two or three years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's an annual programme there in Sarajevo, and I've been I think invited to pretty much all of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you been to any of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a conference here in The Hague at the Peace Palace I think in December of 2008 that I did attend and gave a paper on the issue of the disposition of the archives of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go then to the substance of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we turn to page 3. Sorry, can we -- I hope you've got a paper copy of your expert report in this case, Mr. Donia. That's what I'm referring to. I apologise for being less than clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this is the first title of the report, "Political Ideals of Assembly Leaders and Delegates." And you make the point in the first paragraph there that: "Delegates often assign priority to Serb national interests over other values and ideals as is evident in many of the following excerpts." Just so I understand what it was that you were seeking to do, were you seeking to demonstrate that fact, that Serbs in the Assembly assign priority to their interests over other values and ideals? Is that the substance of the section?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The introduction was subsequent to the selection -- I wrote the introduction subsequent to the selection of the excerpts and was trying to summarise the primary themes that one finds in the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which were, how would you summarise the themes then that this section is supposed to represent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I just wrote it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, is it this then: Serb nationalism and Serb national interests over other values and ideals. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, read the entire paragraph or much of it: "Delegates articulated general political principles as well as commenting on specific issues. They most commonly spoke of their commitment to Serb populist nationalism, but they also embraced fundamental precepts of liberal democratic thought: constitutionalism, the rule of law, and parliamentary governance."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how was it in your mind that you related this to your task of selecting excerpts relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I selected the excerpts under the category of political ideals of Assembly leaders and delegates, and then attempted to summarise the major topics which the delegates addressed in this introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But in your mind how was this relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain behaviour is alleged in the indictment, and I think that this goes to explaining the motivations and the objectives, goals, I would say the philosophical orientation which stood behind the acts alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to the next section. This is the strategic goals, page 17. Now, what were you purporting to do in this section?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I searched for excerpts that reflected the ideas inherent in the six strategic goals that were adopted on May 12th, 1992, and published in November of 1993, with the belief that they did not just spring out of the air in May of 1992, that the ideas were there in somewhat unrefined form, perhaps, before they were actually written down and approved, and that they were repeated, reiterated, and employed to govern the behaviour of the Bosnian Serb government after they were approved and published.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 19, please. And can we also have on e-court Rule 65 ter 1286. And can we go, please, to page ERN 0084-0470. And can we please enlarge the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, if you look at you -- at paragraph 41 of your report have included the second to last paragraph: "Speaking of which, I would like to single out the significance of the area of Northern Bosnia ..." And then the next paragraph, the first three lines are missed out: "I appeal to you to propose in these negotiations such options as would keep BH within the existing borders with possibly new borders in Herzegovina accomplished by peaceful means because force will not do." Is there any reason why you selected the first paragraph before the sentence I've just read out but missed out that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to take a minute to look at this and see if I can recall why I drew the lines around the excerpts where I did. I have to say, it's often a very difficult decision to know exactly how much to take and the temptation is to take a great deal and to lengthen the report and enrich the context and do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just take your time to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just consult with my colleague while that's happening, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any page reference for the B/C/S version? That's what Madam Registrar is asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I am afraid. If I can be forgiven for this one and then make sure that this doesn't happen after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether I'm the person to forgive you but at least to show understanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You know, I think looking at it, it could -- I could very well have included it without -- without changing much. I think the reason I did not include it was it goes off the topic slightly of the actual -- the corridor, which is strategic goal number 2, and goes to the subject of borders in Herzegovina which really were not addressed in a strategic goal with the exception of the Neretva river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to page 20 of the English version. Paragraph -- please could we have on e-court, 587. Rule 65 ter 587, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What page, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. It's page 11 or page ERN -- sorry, if we go on page 11, I think, on the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we can see in paragraph 45 your inclusion of the paragraph. I think that the most fundamental thing which we can find in page 11, the third paragraph, and then the actual words of Krajisnik include the following: "Off the record, there you have agreed to the idea that the BH should be partitioned according to the" -- sorry I've lost myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What page are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 11. What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the second -- the second paragraph on the page there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Let us first have" -- sorry, it's the third paragraph on the page. "Let us" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Let us first have a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I think that the most fundamental..." yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then I'm just reading out the line that was missed out from Mr. Donia's excerpts, which reads four lines into that paragraph. Please, could we go left to the beginning so that we can see the -- "Off the record they have agreed to the idea that these be called states or republics, I'm speaking about the European community which put the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, under lots of pressure to accept this." Is this correct that Krajisnik is referencing what the Bosnian Serbs in the Assembly understood to be the political decision negotiated with the European community acting as the arbiter, if you like?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, what was the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Krajisnik -- Krajisnik is discussing, as you would say the six strategic goals but with reference to what's happening politically with the European community, putting the SDA party under pressure to accept certain Bosnian Serb goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't specifically address the six strategic goals, no. It refers to the EC negotiations that have concluded earlier this day, and he is in very succinct language describing the understanding that he and Karadzic had that -- fundamentally an agreement had been reached for partition according to ethnic principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Krajisnik was saying well this is good, this is consistent with what we wanted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And if we -- perhaps if you just take a moment to read that page 11 in its totality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just lost the text. I just can't -- having great difficulty reading this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could we enlarge the English version at this moment. Is this any better, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Can you go down the page, please, just a bit. I still can't see the entire page. Okay, I've reviewed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 12, please. And page 13 also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about giving a hard copy to Mr. Donia and then resume after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A hard copy of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of what he is reading now and ask him to read it over the break because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're taking -- it's going at a very slow speed at this moment for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I'm still on for finishing within two hours, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which would mean that you would need 45 more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just have something I want to bring to the court's attention before we break, I'm not sure if you are about to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Since it seems that we are going to -- the witnesses scheduled for this week will go into next week, I've just been advised that the witness next week has some medical issues as well, and so the Prosecution is requesting if the Chamber would consider whether it's possible to sit additional sessions next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it would be preferable if we finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no way. If you would look at the Gotovina case scheduling, then you may be aware that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, ten hours a day, to add to ten hours a day would not be a wise thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first have a break, and could you through the Registrar provide Mr. Donia with a copy of the pages you wanted him to read and perhaps also pages still to come, and then we are going to spoil your breaks, Mr. Donia, because Mr. -- I don't know how many other pages you have for the witness to read because that takes less time in court and would bring you down to 35 minutes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My favourite activity is reading these transcripts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do understand. Mr. Jordash, would you have a -- how many do you still have that you want to read major portions by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, this is the largest portion. The rest will be much, much smaller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have them available, could you usually copying takes, I take them that you have them in hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, no, I've been using them -- it may take some time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to -- Mr. Donia, Mr. Jordash is doing his utmost best to provide you to the extent possible, technically possible, with anything he would invite you to read after the break. We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just check on the situation with copies, Mr. Donia, were you given and have you had a chance to read a number of pages from different Assembly minutes? I know our time was short so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just got them a few minutes ago, and I was able to look at a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I think it will speed things up that you've got paper copies anyway. I was asking you to look at 65 ter 587, pages 11 to 13. Did you have a chance to read them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the 11th session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the -- just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one on our screen at this moment is the 11th session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 18th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have indeed read pages 11 through 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 11 to 13, I suggest, contextualises and provides valuable context to what Krajisnik was in fact talking about, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In that it places within context his remarks, at paragraph 45 of your report, into the context of European community or negotiations under the auspices of the European community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. I think the prior comments of Dr. Karadzic also provide substantial context to what Mr. Krajisnik says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, which remarks are these?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in his summary, Karadzic actually addresses what he understands to be the status of the negotiations, and he appears to have the conclusions before him which were also published and very accurately and cautiously goes through and outlines what has been agreed upon and emphasises that it was a basis for further negotiation before turning over the podium to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside and then move on to the next point I want to raise. Please would you turn to paragraph 48 of your report, and this is where Karadzic outlines the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, one very practical question, if you ask the witness whether this contextualises and you give three pages, how is the Chamber at a later stage to be able to evaluate that evidence? Do you want to tender those three pages or the whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, to a degree I'm in Your Honours's hands because what we will do in due course will ourselves go through the Assembly minutes and pull out the excerpts which we say, overall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you want to add to them, perhaps, and then make that bar table submissions to -- in order to contextualise and to be submitted by the parties with their comments. This contextualises paragraph 45 of the expert's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes or perhaps an expert report of our own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at this moment that will follow. You will understand that if we hear this evidence that it's without any meaning if we don't have those paragraphs in one way or another available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, if Your Honour would prefer for example when there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not prefer anything. I just draw your attention to the fact that if the witness says pages 11, 12, and 13 give further context to what I've put in my report, that to evaluate that evidence for the Chamber is impossible if not in one way or another in a summary format through another witness, by bar tabling it, whatever way we have that available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think to save time, I will go down the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 48 of your report deals with Karadzic's outlining of the strategic goals, and we've seen what you say about them in the Karadzic trial, and I just want to take you -- if you just keep a finger in the report at paragraph 48, and then turn to paragraph 242 which deals with something that General Mladic said, if I'm correct, please correct me if I'm not, was said in the same session in response to discussions about the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: People and peoples are not pawns, nor are the keys in ones pockets that can be shifted from here to there, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why you didn't put that into the section detailing the six strategic goals because it appears to me that Mladic's comment about avoiding the shifting of people at the same session the strategic goals were outlined is of some significance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. As I indicated, I think, in the introduction to the report, there are a number of excerpts that could go in two or even three sections and this, you know, is certainly one of them that could equally well fall into the strategic goal section, but he doesn't, I guess I made the decision to put it here because he is really speaking primarily about the conduct of war or the fact that he does not want to have a war against the Muslims as a people or Croats against the people, and it appears to, you know, caution everyone else about the fact that this kind of -- these kinds of forced population movements would be in his view genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, isn't he saying in reference to the first goal of the separation of the national communities that it ought not to involve transfer of populations, that the separation of states is something other than that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't mention the first strategic goal here, he doesn't specifically address it. And I think that's why I put it here rather than under the strategic goal section but it could very well go in the Serb strategic goal section as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the 12th of May, 1992 Assembly was really focused on the strategic goals, and you would accept, wouldn't you, that Mladic was responding to and interpreting his version of a strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. I think there's a lot of things going on at the 16th session including some disagreements between Karadzic and -- or between Mladic and some of the delegates about just how much the military effort should play a role in making these things happen. So I don't think this is him directly, let's say contradicting or disputing the first strategic goal. He is really talking here about -- more about the manner in which it might be -- should not be pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the -- I don't think we are in disagreement. He is not saying let's not pursue that strategic goal, strategic goal 1, or it's not a goal we should aim for. He is saying it's a goal which I understand not to involve the transfer of populations, it's something other than that, a political ideal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was his position at the time Mladic was speaking at this Assembly minute -- Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was either about to be made -- I believe he was about to be made the commander of the VRS which itself was not actually created yet. He was at that time, I believe, the commander of the 2nd military district of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I think is this right, this was one of the first, if not the first, Assembly that he had attended?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's probably right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn -- I think you've got a paper copy of Rule 65 ter 4721, pages 9 to 15, and I just want to look at paragraph 61 of your report in light of this wider context. I don't know -- did you get the chance to -- I don't want to rush you. I know that you were landed with this at the last minute, so, 4721, did you get a chance to read the pages 9 to 15?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you want to just --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm broadly familiar with them, if you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can do it this way then. I want to just have a focus for a moment on the union of three republics peace plan, and if we look at page 9 of 4721, I think we might find some reference and explanation of it. If we look at the second -- the third paragraph on page 9.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second paragraph you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is Karadzic speaking and addressing the 34th session.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he notes at paragraph 3: "One of the most important documents is the constitutional agreement on the Alliance of the BiH republics, i.e., the union of the republics, we can call it like that." Could you just explain briefly what this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you are referring to 65 ter numbers, the Chamber would not immediately know what you are -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could give the number of the session and the date so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It's the 34th session, 27th of October to 1st of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's page 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The union of the three republics was the successor peace plan to the Vance-Owen Plan which failed when it was rejected by the Bosnian Serbs in May of 1993. At the time Karadzic is speaking here, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first have it on our screen because I don't think that we have it at this moment. I think we are still on the 11th session of the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I should have asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could we ask for -- I think it's 65 -- it was 4721. 65 ter 4721.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 4721, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have that on our screen, page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that 4721 is the 18th of March, 11th session, so therefore -- could you please check, Mr. Jordash, whether you have the right reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm surprised at that because it's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Because I've got 4721 on my notes, and we've just checked over the break that 4721 is this and we've got the B/C/S page numbers too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we are right actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it with a soft voice. The problem is the Chamber is unable to search on 65 ter numbers. That's -- this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have on our screen, perhaps with ERN numbers, we have starts with 0190-4669, that's what we have on our screen as the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What we need, Your Honour, is 0215-0508, of the English, is the English ERN. And the B/C/S ERN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now we have the -- Madam Registrar, under what 65 ter number is the document which we have now on our screen entered into e-court?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the page 1 of 65 ter 4721 and before that was page 9 of the same 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That comes really as a surprise because when I click through the cover page of the previous document was still the 18th of March, 11th session. So we have to carefully check that there are no mistakes. We are now in the right document. We move to page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 9 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There must have been made a mistake somewhere. Your 65 ter number was right, we are now on the relevant -- no, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we can, to shortcut things, go to -- straight to page 11 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Mr. Karadzic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if you've had during that time, Mr. Donia, a chance to read through the pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but the right page is not yet -- page 13 is not yet on the screen. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At this stage, I mean, if we look through the 9 to 15, there's a general agreement, is this right, being expressed by Karadzic concerning the, if you like, congruence between the union of republics' plan and the strategic goals and Karadzic is making the point, and this is most clearly made at page 15, that apart from strategic aim 5, the union peace plan provides pretty much everything else of the Serbian strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the union of three republics' peace plan involved not only creating corridors and taking land from Muslims, but it also involved the vice-versa, the same creating corridors for the Muslims and taking land from the Serbs, and we see this in these pages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the case. It actually had fewer enclaves and corridors than did the predecessor plan, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, but still adhered to that same basic formula of trying to carve out an ethnic map with consideration to these issues of contiguity and compactness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And just finally, sir, would you agree that pages 9 to 15 contextualise the discussions concerning the Bosnian Serbs strategic goals in light of the political agreement which are being sought to reach through the union of three republics' peace plan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under negotiation I think at that point and not yet agreed upon, but I agree with the rest of your formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That does indeed contextualise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry? That --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does indeed contextualise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can turn now, please, in e-court and in the paper copies to Rule 65 ter 1320.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Jordash, that would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I have them in front of me, I see those numbers, but we cannot -- what's the date [overlapping speakers]?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Sorry. It's session 30th session, 5th to 6th of May, 1993, and it's a conversation -- or it's a speech by Milosevic. And it's page 113 that I'm ... This doesn't seem to be the -- the right page. In fact I need -- sorry, we'll have to do this on the screen, I'll need page 96, which is where we'll find the speech by Milosevic, but then the speech goes on, and I want to make sure that we understand that this is the continuation of the Milosevic speech at 113. And the B/C/S is 80 to 81. Maybe we can shortcut this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to paragraph 88 of your report, Mr. Donia, you deal with the speech by Milosevic when he attended on the one occasion to address the Assembly about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And maybe you know the Assembly minutes well enough to agree with me that Milosevic also says during this speech "everything needs to be sacrificed for the people except for the people themselves" when urging the Bosnian Serbs to accept the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you are really confusing me. On page 113 of this document, Milosevic is not speaking, so therefore could you please be a bit more organised that we -- it's not just listening to words but also try to understand what is said and to be able to follow the excerpts. And on page 113, I see that Mr. Gavric starts speaking halfway the page, and on the previous page we see Miroslav Vjestica speaking. So if you want to be taken seriously, we want to take you seriously by following what you are presenting to the Court, then please be precise. It's not the first time today, so I apologise for the slight irritation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I apologise. I think if we go to page 96 to 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 96 to 97 of this document, which is -- let me just see what we have there. Yes, we have that now on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can we get the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page in B/C -- I think I can leave this point because the witness has already confirmed. I don't think we need to turn to this page, I've got the wrong page number in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So rather than wasting any more time, the witness has agreed that Milosevic said that during the speech and that was the only point I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we turn to paragraph 197 of your report, Mr. Donia. And it's the 32nd session, 19 to 20 of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please refer to a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for context we are now dealing with the section of your report which deals with the police MUP and state security services. Do you have the paper copies there, Mr. Donia, 1324? The pages I'm interested in are pages 55 to -- I think I'm going to shortcut things by just asking you to read 55 to 65 of the English, which is 37 to 40 of the B/C/S and just ask you the same question, whether this contextualises what was happening with the security services within Bosnia, the Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll permit me to go rapidly through it, I believe I can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Dr. Donia is doing that, I just want to state the Prosecution's position would be that there are a number of experts coming in the future that the Prosecution would have no objection to -- once the witness begins to testify, if counsel wants to submit through the Court Officer some documents for the witness to read overnight, the Prosecution would have no objection to that so perhaps with future experts it might go quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on what I've read, I would concur that it provides context to the excerpt in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And Jovo Mijatovic, which is speaking from page 56 onwards about the security services, who was Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a delegate. I don't -- can't go beyond that. I don't know what position he made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the discussion concerning the police and the security services was, if I can label it generically, was a discussion about the fragmentation of the security services and the need to bring it under unified command? I know that's a broad generalisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's a valid generalisation. There are other issues discussed as well of the, let's say, ineffectiveness of the police and security forces, but your statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the discussions that took place within the Assembly concerning the police and the security services were -- and the need to bring them under a unified command, were focused on the Bosnian Serbs, they were not focused on other intelligence or security services, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were primarily focused on the Bosnian Serbs, but reading through, I see some of the issues that they discussed here in fact related to Serbian MUP and perhaps not identified as such but also kind of reached over the border, so primarily focused on the Bosnian Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when the Serbian services are discussed, it's largely in relation to the exchange of certain information, intelligence information relating to military operations; would you agree with that as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, it is focused on that. It's also focused on these instances of corruption and free movement of goods without being taxed and the theft of the automobiles, things like that.
