So certainly one of the topics that receives primary attention here is the security service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I'm coming to a close, if I can just have a minute just to check something. Two more things if I may. Could we turn to paragraph 226 of your report. And it's the reference to the 19th session, 12th of August, 1992. And it's 2372, 65 ter 2372.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I just wanted to ask you about the reference there to the paramilitaries. I don't know if you know this again from your recollection, but do you recall General Gvero being present during some of the Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall him being present at a number of Assembly meetings. I can't specifically attest to whether he was present at this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall him speaking about paramilitaries and the need for the Main Staff of the VRS to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't specifically recall that discussion or assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was Gvero's position at that time, do you know, around this point in time, mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a senior commander. I believe he was Chief of Staff of the VRS, but if not that a senior commander and perhaps deputy commander too to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask one of the final topics, could we turn please to 233 of your report. And a discussion about the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the discussion about the Red Berets, as far as you recall, from the Assembly minutes focus on it being a problem from the RS Army and they whoever they were being subordinated to that army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not want to go too far without refreshing my memory by actually looking at the passage. But as I recall, the concern was in this particular instance, the killing of this policeman and the threat that Red Berets pose to civilians and domestic tranquility in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was accepted amongst those present during the Assembly session that they were a -- effectively a unit of the RS Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you can see from 233, the excerpt that you placed within the report, appears to suggest that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojinovic certainly concluded that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Presumably if you'd seen something else in the Assembly minutes you would have put that in given you were putting in issues relevant to the indictment, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to make a number of cuts along the line and I -- I can't absolutely guarantee that there isn't something there pertaining to the Red Berets that I have not included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were aware from reading the indictment that the Red Berets was figured largely -- large in this case, as an organisation that allegedly run organised commanded by the accused?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, I've got nothing further. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apologies for the disorganised nature of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's say it was the first session after the recess, but as time proceeds, the level of organisation may improve as well. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you are cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia. First of all I would like to put several questions to you relating to a topic that was partly addressed by my learned friend Mr. Jordash. Could you please, in as much detail as possible, explain to us and describe for us what the Office of the Prosecutor this particular team asked of you and how they defined your task in preparation for your expert report, what it is that this specific team asked of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team asked me to survey the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions through its minutes and transcripts, from the beginning until the August session of 1996 with a view toward making a -- excerpting limited passages which shed light on events and developments referenced in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, were you asked to focus on specific events and to focus on specific individuals, were there such requests?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only insofar as I was asked to review the indictment and pay attention to individuals that were named in the indictment insofar as there was substantive information about them in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you only shown the indictment and were you only told to look for the relevant matters yourself or were you directed to specific passages of the indictment where you were told that you were supposed to bring in information to corroborate and uphold certain elements of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such instructions were given to me. I believe I looked at the indictment online in San Diego without having any discussion with a member of the Prosecutor team about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there any sort of written communication between you and the Office of the Prosecutor defining your tasks or were you merely given verbal instructions and the indictment, and were you only told to produce an expert report based on the indictment itself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given verbal instructions and a contract to do the background search of the sessions and produce the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you produce several versions of the report for this case or is there only one version; namely, the one we are discussing today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I had drafts in my computer as I was bringing this together, but there is only one final version and that's the one before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Petrovic is interested to know whether any of the drafts were discussed between you and the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not discuss the drafts with anyone on the Prosecution team. I did have a -- a contact, basically a research person in the OTP who assisted in making sure I got all the sessions of the -- of both the minutes and the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that seems to be a matter a bit different. When you provided -- did you provide a draft to the Office of the Prosecution, well, let's say the first draft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide any draft prior to this final version to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but let me qualify that I did provide drafts to that research person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the research person was employed by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Employed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I understand that to be a direct communication with someone employed in the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But there was no -- we didn't discuss the substantive content of the report. It was all directed toward technical issues of making sure that I had the sessions and had the correct corresponding English and B/C/S. There were some sessions that had not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So nothing else was discussed as the completeness of your source material as far as the sessions are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever any suggestion to add something to what was in the draft that by the research assistant or to take out any portion of what you had included in the draft that you communicated to that research person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify one matter. You provided one of the draft versions of your report to that researcher from the OTP who, in my understanding, was merely required to provide you with technical assistance. My question for you is why did you have to provide him with a draft of your report at all if what you required was merely technical assistance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was her, not him. The problems surfaced mainly around translations. There were a number of passages that I selected that had not yet been translated. I submitted those passages to the representative of the OTP to be sure that they were translated. I submitted passages or excerpts that had been translated poorly or weren't up to my satisfaction. And so there was plenty of give and take and feedback on those issues, but the content of the -- the selection of the excerpts never came into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To what extent does the version, the draft that you provided to the researcher of the OTP differ from the one that we have before us now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that I provided a draft. I provided portions of or selected excerpts to this person. There is one final document in its entirety that came together, that I brought together, at the end of this process after all the translations were in order and all the numbering was straightened out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the first and only time that you provided a draft was the full version that we have before us today, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the minutes that you reviewed, how voluminous were they? How many pages did they number?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question. I have not counted them. I believe them to be in the area of 6.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't number the -- count the pages and you probably didn't attempt to gauge how many hours of discussions were recorded in these minutes. Do you have an estimate of hours, days, or perhaps even weeks of uninterrupted debates that were reviewed and were the subject of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never tried to estimate the amount of time that this talking actually consumed, but it would be in the certainly hundreds of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you lack any of the minutes? Did you have all the material that you needed among the papers that were placed at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did lack some of the minutes and in fact some of the transcripts as well. So yes, I actually found it a major task to inventory everything that I had, identify things that were missing, and then requesting those things from the OTP representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And finally you did receive all the material, if I've understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm still missing some minutes, and that is probably -- that could be because minutes were not taken or preserved or turned over to the OTP, and it could be simply that the OTP couldn't locate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the minutes were, or at least the time-period they referred to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In percentages, what the volume of the material would be? We have the sessions from the 1st to the 63rd, and how many in your estimation are missing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there's any full session that's missing. The minutes are typically very abbreviated and distinctly uninformative. If there are 10, 15 sessions for which there are not minutes, that would be about my guess of how many of the minutes are missing. But I don't believe there's any transcript missing. There were also four extraordinary sessions, one celebratory session, in the course of this time-frame, so the total number gets to I think about 70, and the one session that does not exist, I've never found the transcript or the minutes of the session is the 15th session which was held on April 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, earlier today you told us that the material that was pinpointed in your report was contrary to the case put forward by the OTP. Can you tell us and refer us specifically to the material that you indicated in your report and which goes against the Prosecution case? You told us this and its recorded in the transcript today at page 7.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've misrepresented what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything which you say could be a misrepresentation, let's look at the literal text of what you said. Mr. Petrovic, you say page 7 of today's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the end of page 6 and at the beginning of page 7, Your Honours. I may have simplified it a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, I'll read it to you: "Could I suggest," that was Mr. Jordash's question, "that the reason that you didn't take the approach you've taken with other cases, other than Milosevic, was that in fact you considered along with the Prosecution that this was the best way of supporting the indictment?" And your answer was: "No, that's not the case. I think the excerpts themselves will tell you that the purpose of this particular report was to shed light on a lot of different events, attitudes, some of which in fact go in directions quite apart from what the Prosecution might argue in some instances." And what Mr. Petrovic is asking you, whether you could give examples of excerpts which, as you said, go in directions quite apart from what the Prosecution might argue. Could you give examples of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could probably go through and find something in about a third of the -- maybe even half of the entries, but I would start with number one with Krajisnik's very precise description of the issue of the Bosnian Assembly and the Council for National Equality, which is -- doesn't figure at all, as far as I can see, in the Prosecution thinking or the actual case. I think we spoke of one yesterday when we were looking at the great Dusan's empire. The point that Karadzic made in that statement and makes repeatedly in the Assembly is that he wanted it to give up land in the negotiation process in order to achieve peace. That is, to me, just -- I can look through these and see that's pretty much an irrefutable conclusion that goes, I think, in quite a different direction than the Prosecution argues it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you have your report before you. You said that you would start from item 1, and if you say that there's many of them, I suppose you wouldn't find it difficult to find the next example of such an instance contained in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, number -- I point out here number -- it's -- excuse me just a second, Your Honour. It's Mr. Buha in the 4th session giving this very succinct statement about the relationship between civil society and national identity. I don't hear anything about that from the Prosecution. I think it's a strong affirmation of that principle on his part. It's -- certainly I put it there because I find it to be the most, let's say, compelling statement of that difference that I found in all the Bosnian Serb Assembly minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to paragraph 9 of your report, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say "contrary to the Prosecution case," what is the case of the Prosecution on this particular score and what is your finding which is contrary to their case, and I'm asking about the issue of national and civic identity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Prosecution's case is, Mr. Petrovic, is not for the witness to testify about. What he can tell us is to what extent the matters he addresses in his report, in his opinion, are supportive or undermining for what he reads in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have not been as precise as I would have wished. I'm asking him not to explain for us what the Prosecution case is, but his understanding of the Prosecution case where he sees a discrepancy between that case and the findings he draws in the report we have before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now we are moving a bit from what the witness testified on page 6 or 7, that is that he said moves away from more or less, not to say that it contradicts or -- but I take it that Mr. Donia has meanwhile understood more or less what Mr. Petrovic would like to know, and if you please in that understanding could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- really don't know what the Prosecution's argument is vis-a-vis nationalism or what I call Serb populist nationalism. I'm sure they don't use that term, or I have not seen that term used, but I don't see the -- I don't see that issue entering into the Prosecution discussion at all; that is, the difference between a civic understanding and the Bosnian Serb populist nationalism. The Prosecution in general seems to completely neglect the role of civic option political forces in the conflict, and that would certainly be one of the things that I hope I've illuminated here in part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer well that you say that you took a broader approach to what is found in the indictment but in a -- where the indictment gives a rather incomplete picture of what really happened in society in all its elements that is military, political, civic society?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that it's -- my frame of mind when I was going about this was to say I want to hear how these people expressed this in their own words, in their own vocabulary, and insofar as they explain their motivations, explain their values, orientations, I want to capture that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so I'd -- it is -- I'd have to say it's a somewhat difficult question to separate what I have here, which is very, very diffused, I mean, it's a very comprehensive, but not a wholly consistent story with what the Prosecution would present it. I could illustrate with, say, great Serbia, I mean, I think that I hear a lot about great Serbia from the Prosecution from time to time. I don't see it very much in the actual expressions of Bosnian Serbs. It's there occasionally, but very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, may I invite you to phrase your questions as precisely as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I would like us to look at paragraph 25 of your report, which is the 20th session. There the Assembly deputies discuss the amendments to the constitution of the republic of Republika Srpska, and among them the amendment which provides for the borders of Republika Srpska to be changed only by plebiscite and with a qualified majority. My question is to your knowledge, was this amendment ever applied in practice? Was this constitutional amendment ever effectively implemented?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Bosnian Serbs themselves saw the referendum or the plebiscite after the Assembly session on the 5th and 6th of May as an implementation of this amendment, the Article 2, in which they asked for a vote on the peace plan which would have, of course, changed and/or established borders. So in that plebiscite, yes, they were implementing this provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 5th and 6th of May of what year, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- they later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- voted -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, are you sure that the referendum you referred to was called pursuant to this constitutional amendment and the specific provision envisaging a two-thirds majority of votes and envisaging this possibility to change borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three-quarter vote. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are not sure what the constitutional basis of the referendum was, the one that you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd have to go to the specific Assembly session to see what constitutional provision they cited in authorising the holding of the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I take it that you did not put a question to the witness without at least some knowledge. Could you inform the Chamber or could you help the Chamber to find whether or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Save for my interpretation of the constitutional text and the knowledge of the events, no, I don't have any additional information. I can't offer anything else. Your Honour, I should like to continue. I'm interested in paragraph 26. It's a session which took place in January 1993 and where Krajisnik said that it was the position of the Assembly that the Muslims were a communist creation and that they were a religious group of Turkish orientation. They are unbelievers, a nation that is not a nation, that is to say a nation that would like to be a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question for you, Mr. Donia, is as follows: In the transcripts of the Assembly sessions, did you ever come across a piece of information or a fact that the state policy of Serbia or those who represented the state policy of Serbia and Yugoslavia at the time shared the view put forth by Momcilo Krajisnik about the inception and existence of Bosniak or Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraph 27, Karadzic speaking, the 25th session, and his words Karadzic says that for a civic type of state, it is the Muslim side -- the Muslim side advocated a civic state counting on its birth-rate and their large numbers. Had we accepted the Muslim proposal, the statehood constitutiveness of the Serbian people would have been lost forever and we would have become a national minority in a Islamic society. Now, in these minutes, did you come across any representative of the state organ of Serbia or Yugoslavia shares this position about the Muslim mentality in Bosnia-Herzegovina as expressed by Karadzic? Muslim natality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across a speech by a representative from Serbia. I can't recall and I probably couldn't come quickly to it whether he held any official position or not. I believe he was an academic in academy or something like that which expressed similar views, but I can't point you to any place that a representative of the government of Serbia indicated that they shared these views.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. I think I was precise in my question and I meant the representative of the authorities. I'm not interested in academics, writers, or anybody else, but just state authority and state policy and the representatives thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honour, may I have your instructions with respect to time, shall we take a break? When is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are about to have a break. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure but let's say 45 minutes at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I read from yesterday's transcript, up to one hour. You've taken now 35 minutes. You are asking for 45 more minutes. That is not up to one hour. That is well over your estimate, Mr. Petrovic. Could I get a more realistic estimate which fits within your time estimate you've given yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 20 minutes. It's a matter of 20 minutes. Now, it's difficult for me to assess how much more time I will need, but with your permission those extra 20 minutes I don't think will change anything of substance. I'll try and get through it as quickly as possible but it will be difficult, so I do feel that I need these extra 20 minutes, and I hope they won't change anything. But I'll try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They change the start of the testimony of the next witness, Mr. Petrovic. That's what is changing. Let me see, you said yesterday up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber extends your estimate and allows you 1 hour and 10 minutes, you've taken 35 minutes if I'm well because Mr. Jordash stopped at a quarter to 1.00, you've taken 35 minutes, therefore you get another 35 minutes after the break. We resume at a quarter to 1.00 and then you have until 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, as matters stand now, how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Then it doesn't make much sense to start with the next witness perhaps for five or ten minutes at the very end because if Mr. Petrovic would go on until 20 minutes past 1.00 then perhaps some questions from the Bench, you would have five minutes then we would have 10 minutes for the next witness, 10 to 15 minutes, that might not be a good thing to do. If at least the parties would be able to -- the next witness would take how much for cross-examination, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I said three yesterday, but I think probably more like 2 and a half, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half. Mr. Petrovic, how much time would you need for the next witness in cross-examination -- or Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, two to two and a half hours. I'll do my best to make it two hours, but I want to leave that margin. And I'll try and see if Mr. Jordash and I can share some topics, so to speak, and then I'll be able to complete my examination within the two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances and having consulted my colleagues and knowing how many questions there will be from the Bench, it does make sense to start with the next witness. We'll have a break, we'll resume at quarter to 1.00. Mr. Petrovic, you'll have until 20 minutes past 1.00 and we would have 15 minutes to start the cross-examination of the next witness. We resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are extended to 25 minutes past 1.00, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not your mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, shall we continue? Would you take a look at paragraph 82 of your statement, which is the speech delivered by Biljana Plavsic at the 22nd session where she refers to letters she sent and she goes on to say: "I wanted to find people who fought for the Serbian cause who want to fight in the territory of Republika Srpska. These letters were also sent to the Soviet Union, they were also sent to Seselj and Arkan and Jovic, whatever suits you, and now you can accuse me of that. With respect I want to clear this up because this is the second time, Mr. Minister," et cetera. And then there was a round of applause from the deputies after that. Now, Mr. Donia, can you tell us whether in the continuation of this session or during the material period of time that we are referring to whether you came across condemnation of any kind by the deputies from the appeal made by Plavsic to Arkan, Jovic, Seselj, and so on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we then conclude that the deputies supported the appeal launched by Plavsic to these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can conclude that all of them did. Clearly some of them did because they applauded, but I can't conclude that all the deputies did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was not of course that all of them did. My question was whether you agree that not only if we look at this within this context, but in general terms, broader terms, that the appeal was an expression of the majority political will in Republika Srpska at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to paragraph 87. Velimir Lukic, the newly designated prime minister of Republika Srpska is saying that between the Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a credit system will be set up with a unified monetary and credit systematised and so on. Now, my question to you is whether any of these systems were actually set up, so customs, taxes, et cetera? Were any of those regimes put into effect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to paragraph 117 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, monetary system is not the same as a tax or custom system, that -- I just wanted to draw your attention to that. And since in your previous question you also sought to rely on unsourced knowledge of the witness, which is very much against what Mr. Jordash thinks is appropriate, I just want to invite you again to be very precise in your phrasing of the questions and of the sources you ask the witness to rely on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for that. I did indicate the paragraphs and so I thought that was sufficient, but I was actually asking only what is mentioned in the paragraph, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at paragraph 117 now, please. And in paragraph 117, a proposal for the declaration on the unification of the Republic of Serbia, the republic -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina is being discussed. Now, Mr. Donia, my question is this: To the best of your knowledge, was this declaration ever discussed in the Assembly of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, the contents of this declaration, was any of that ever put into practice? Was it ever realised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us if we look at the time when this declaration was being proposed whether this was happening precisely at the time when because the plan of the Contact Group had not been accepted, a blockade was underway along the Drina and other border crossings from the SRJ into Republika Srpska? I'm just asking you about the time-frame here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was indeed made in the time-frame where a blockade had been announced along the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, I'd like us next to look at paragraph 132 where Karadzic is quoted, and it refers to the events after the fall of Western Slavonija, and he is recounting the meeting he had with President Milosevic, and then he says what they discussed, and then he goes on to say: "We asked to go to Orasje, and for the 11th Corps to go to Spacva forest, and for us to meet and tear off a chunk of Croatia and charge for it, and then link up Eastern Slavonia with the Republika Srpska. President Milosevic was against that." Do we conclude from this that Karadzic's request for an escalation of the war on the territory of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, that that demand was rejected by the SRJ or rather President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By President Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, paragraph 141. The quotation is from October 1995 and what Vojo Kupresanin said. Can you tell us who Vojo Kupresanin was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin was a delegate in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. He was the first president of the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina, and later became the director of Serbian radio TV in the RS. He was relieved from that position, so I believe at this point in time he was just a delegate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now take a look at paragraph 150. Karadzic speaking, and he says: "In 1991 we said in the Presidency of Yugoslavia it was all recorded and stayed there. We said now we have a chance to come out on our borders and form a state. They will criticise us, they will attack us, and then they will recognise us. There was no masculine strength or a statements' vision to do it at the time." Now, studying the thousands of pages of these minutes, who does Karadzic have in mind when he says there was no masculine strength or a statements' vision to carry out the unification that he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is referring here to members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about a Presidency member at the time that all the representatives stepped down from the Presidency of Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia, so it was only within that context that this was discussed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the so-called Rump Presidency from which those other delegates had withdrawn. I don't think they had resigned but they had withdrawn from the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us under whose dominant influence did this Rump Presidency exist? Which political personage was it under?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, paragraph 154. Krajisnik speaking, he a talking about regionalisation, and he says: "It is our goal to -- and we are talking about November 1991. "It is our goal to decentralise all republican funds, to keep most of the income of citizens legal entities in their municipalities, regions, and autonomous districts so that only limited contributions are paid to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Does this request for regionalisation as defined here -- or rather is it a frequent demand in complex states where decentralisation is called for, first of all, for in the fiscal field? Is this something that is unusual or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And specific only to this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would seem that it's outside the expertise of this particular expert. It seems to be [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I'd like us to look at paragraph 173.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Karadzic speaking. On the 24th of March, 1992, on the take-over of Zvornik municipality. Among other things, he says: "All -- at that moment, all Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory and municipality concerned. The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian municipality of Zvornik." And my question to you, Mr. Donia, is this: In the transcript, apart from this piece of information, did you come across any other information whereby the taking over of Zvornik was planned or carried out by somebody from the Republic of Serbia? In the transcripts before you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I have seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to paragraph 175. The deputy there is Miroslav Vjestica, and he says: "I did not write any conclusion, however, from the discussions we held it follows that this Assembly should adopt a conclusion which instructs the prime minister of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the ministers to prepare by Friday an operational plan for assuming power; that is, for establishing power in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Donia, my question is this, in the transcripts that we have before us, did you find a piece of information or a note stating that some organ of the Republic of Serbia took part in preparing a plan for assuming power in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 235 next, please. Karadzic speaking in April 1995. "A distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA. What could be withdrawn was withdrawn and distributed to the Serbian -- to the people in the Serbian areas, but it was the SDS which organised the people and created the army. That was an army." Mr. Donia, my question is this: In the transcripts did you come across any piece of information or note or uttered word that the MUP of the Republic of Serbia had taken part in the distribution of weapons in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the initial stages of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 199 next, please. We discussed this yesterday. Ratko Adzic speaking and he talks about the presence of certain services and says that one of the intelligence services was Tajfun, and it, truth be told, worked for a number of sides. In the transcripts, did you ever come across any information about what other sides this intelligence centre Tajfun worked for that Adzic mentions here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in connection with paragraph 233, it refers to the killing of a policeman in Brcko, it would seem, and my question is this: Do you know anything about the circumstances of that killing, who was killed, how, when, a part from what it says in this paragraph, the one that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, I believe yesterday, the several delegates were aware of and concerned with this murder and directed inquiries to Dr. Vojinovic because they wanted to know more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you know anything more about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what the delegates raised and what's answered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me -- no, I'll withdraw that question. After this session, and we are talking about the 36th session, did you anywhere in these minutes come across any mention of Red Berets in any way and in any context.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. There were -- I recall there were a number of references to Red Berets in the minutes. I can't recall whether they were before this or after this, and I do recall that they provided very little information about the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there was information, any information, didn't you consider that since you were aware of the indictment and what it contains, if you went through all those pages, wouldn't it have been logical for you to extract those portions and to have presented them to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When there is a mere mention of something with no accompanying information or explanation, I don't deem that -- I didn't deem that to be -- to merit inclusion in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your work, do you use electronic search modes for looking through the material?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many hits when you typed in Red Berets did you find in those 6.000 pages of the minutes that we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are largely not searchable and certainly they -- at the time I prepared this report, the search capabilities of Word 2010 were not yet available. So I don't know how many hits there would have been. I never searched for Red Berets. I could only search for them in a single session in any case, and as I say, my best recollection is the words appear a couple of times without substantive information attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I agree that the 1992 copies can't be searched, but you compiled your report using English translations, and that was certainly possible such research and searches could have been conducted, so why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you weren't there, you don't know whether it was possible or not, and I will tell you it was not possible to search them universally for the terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what you searched for while you were going through the document page by page, you didn't record that and can't now tell us so that we can see where mention is made of those Red Berets, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had recourse to my computer and an hour to check the various sources that I took these notes in, I might be able to, but sitting here, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were preparing for this trial, it never occurred you to that this might be relevant for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if we want to look at it, it's an easy job to do. The point is clear, you say Mr. Donia should have done it. He hasn't done it. If it's of interest to know, let's do the job then. I could do it in two hours. Cut and paste all the, make it a one 6.000-page document, I take it all of them are available in English by now and in a kind of word format, search for it, and you'll know whether it's 20 or 100. Let's not -- your point is clear, if it's useful or relevant information, let's try to get it. If it's not, let's leave it to the criticism. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since I have very little time left, Mr. Donia, can you in the briefest of terms tell us something about the Vance-Owen Plan. First off, does the plan imply the cantonal arrangement of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's someone typing in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can even tell you, who it is. It's Mr. Bakrac who is sitting next to Mr. Petrovic. You see an analytical mind helps us out, but he will stop for awhile. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic. Could you please respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, some people referred to it as a cantonal plan, but in reality, the ten units that were created were called provinces, and the provinces 3, 8, and 10 were to fall under Croat governance, provinces 2, 4, and 6 under Serb governance. The three others under Muslim governance, and the Sarajevo area was to be demilitarised and shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I highly appreciate your answer, but I urge you to give me brief answers in view of the shortage of time. Second question, does the Vance-Owen Plan provide for the existence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an international legal entity in the full sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It provides for it as an international legal entity. I'm not sure I would say in the full sense of the word because it's international -- it's actual legal jurisdiction was extremely limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would it therefore remain as one state or as two states or as ten states, that's my question? What was envisaged, does it rise up to the attribution of a state or to the attributes of a state, yes or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question because it's -- it would -- I think cause me to draw a conclusion about what constitutes a international legal entity, and I don't think I could do that, certainly not without some research anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Does the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan imply a mass scale international military presence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it mass scale, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it imply an international military presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear that we're talking about past tense here, it would have entailed an international military presence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Contact Group Plan, I have the same questions in respect of it. Does it have the attributes of a state or does it provide for an international presence -- or, rather, can you first answer this question so I do not put compound questions to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Contact Group Plan certainly provides Bosnia-Herzegovina with more attributes of a state than the Vance-Owen Plan did. And it also presupposed the -- an international military presence to implement the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Contact Group Plan, both these plans were agreed to by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia tried to work on Republika Srpska in terms of accepting these plans or modifying them. Can you please answer with a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part of your question, the answer is certainly no -- certainly yes, I'm sorry, the answer is certainly yes. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did work on leaders of the Republika Srpska to accept the plan. I don't know whether the FRY actually agreed to the plan in the final analysis. They certainly promoted it and supported it and initialled it and encouraged its adoption at the meeting in Athens, but I just don't know whether they ultimately approved it once the Bosnian Serbs had declined to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Based on the acceptance of the Contact Group Plan in 1994, was the regime of sanctions imposed on the FRY eased and were observers, international observers deployed to border crossings between Republika Srpska and the FRY as a result? If we can have your short answer, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You explained for us the content of the Vance-Owen Plan and the Contact Group Plan. Will you agree that none of the six strategic objectives contained in paragraph 48 of your report were implemented or materialised by -- through the acceptance of either of these plans, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. I think you could say that objective number 1 was realised or realised in large measure by both plans. Would have been realised in large measure had they been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm looking at the clock, last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only have five or six questions left and I really appeal to you to allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you've asked for the last ten minutes questions about the content of the Vance-Owen Plan and of all that I take it that what's the content of it, military presence or not, is not in dispute at all. You could have easily agreed whether or not in the Vance-Owen Plan you find provision for military presence, for example. That's just looking at the text and...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution won't object to the admission of the Vance-Owen Plan if that's what Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you've wasted most of your time by asking questions which were easily to agree upon. The content of plans, if you want to use your time in that way, you are free to do it, but I think the time-limits were clearly set. Your last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot put my last question because I can't choose between the ones I have. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Re-examination by Dr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, at page 69, line 18 of today's transcript, Mr. Petrovic said to you that you compiled your report using the English translations of the minutes. My question to you is did you work primarily with the original stenographic notes in the language in which the speakers were speaking, or did you wait and work from the English translation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Largely from the original Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to paragraph 173 of your report, Mr. Petrovic at transcript page 66 drew your attention to the 12th session held on the 24th of March 1992 where in which was discussed the take-over of Zvornik. How long before the actual take-over of Zvornik was this discussion, if you are able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about nine days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Given the context of the entire discussion, does this passage refer to Zvornik alone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This passage refers to all the municipalities in which the Bosnian Serbs were planning to assume control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, at page 41 of today's transcript, line 6 to 10, Mr. Jordash gave you or asked you to comment on a quote made by Mr. Milosevic in the 30th session. And to recall that quote for you, it was quote: "Everything needs to be sacrificed for the people, except for the people themselves." Do you recall that quote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was taken a bit out of context. Can I ask you, looking at the entire speech that Milosevic made at that time, when he refers to "people," who is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is referring to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And can you contextualise that statement, when he is saying that we cannot sacrifice the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was referring both to the people of the Republic of Serbia, whom he was very concerned about suffering under the sanctions regime, and the Serbs of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then the final question that I have for you is at -- relates to paragraph 150 of your report, and Mr. Petrovic at transcript page 65, lines 1 to 5, asked you to comment on a particular passage of Mr. Karadzic. And I'll read the passage that I want you to give further explanation of: "They will criticise us, they will attack us, and then they will recognise us." Can you please place that in context and explain what Mr. Karadzic is referring to with those words?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context he is expressing the idea which he expressed also on a number of other occasions, that it was best to make a move, take territory, and then essentially present the European community and US with a fait accompli, and then they would recognise Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Donia, I have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take you to paragraph 137 of your report. You use that paragraph to explain the changing relationship between Karadzic and Milosevic. And you said, while you see here, he is not equal anymore. I'm now summarising what you said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I read the whole of paragraph 137, it's -- it gives me the impression that he makes a distinction between his personal relationship between Karadzic and Milosevic where there's still no inequality, that he is free to say that he is a fully equal partner in the communications, but if it comes to joint delegations, that there they -- there is a division of labour, that one of them, in this case more or less naturally, Milosevic would be the leader. Therefore seeing those two elements, I have some difficulties in explaining where the earlier reference you gave was also part of a personal relationship, that it really reflects a change. I'm talking about this source which you invoked --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in order to explain that. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I must reach out a little bit beyond the specific quote here to explain that starting with the terms of address, they really were not equal. And that was true in their -- all of their conversations that we have records of. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short here. You say my conclusion is based primarily on other knowledge I have and is not that clearly reflected here; although, with that other knowledge you would interpret this as a reflection of that changing relationship?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I could happily present the evidence of that, if Your Honour wished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm not seeking that. I'm just asking myself whether you would you agree with me that there's a distinction made here between personal relationship in which, whether true or not, Mr. Karadzic still takes the position that he is at an equal footing with Mr. Milosevic, although that that's not in a joint delegation, although you consider this, not for the personal relationship, certainly not to be the accurate situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. That's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions. Any questions triggered by the re-examination or by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague. I'd like to thank you for having answered all the questions by the parties and from the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Donia out of the courtroom and escort the next witness into the courtroom. Before we start the cross-examination of the next witness, I would just like to remind the parties that P53 was marked for identification because the Prosecution -- the Defence had not had sufficient time to review this additional information. Any views now on the admissibility of P53, additional information in relation witness B-215? If not, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would I be able to address you on that next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First thing I'll be in a position to answer that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, although there has been sufficient time to prepare for it, but any view already from the Simatovic Defence? P53 MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We have seen the proofing note dated the 25th of August, 2009, we have gone through it, and we will cross-examine the witness on the evidence he gave at the time but not the proofing note but the new statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what date did you mention, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I'm right, it's the 24th and the 25th of August, 2009. P53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I see that we have some six or five minutes left and the witness still has to come into the courtroom. I have a certain idea of how I'm approaching this examination, and I have trouble deciding how I'm going to start now and have to stop without in fact damaging the way I intend to examine. Perhaps we can let the witness in and we can have preliminary questions, but there are some substantial and essential issues that I will not be able to finish in several minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Find suitable subjects for the next 8 minutes and -- I do not understand why the witness is not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber together with the Registry will work on a more efficient use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Witness, you appear again before this court. I would like to ask you to again make the solemn declaration you made when you came to The Hague and first testified. Could you please repeat my words: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the witness on the right channel? Yes. Could you please make again the solemn declaration you've made at the beginning of your testimony when you first appeared before this court. Mr. Usher, would you please hand out the text of the solemn declaration to the witness in his own language. Could you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. We left off last time you were here with the examination-in-chief. There are no further questions for you by the Prosecution. That means that you now appeared in order to be cross-examined. May I repeat to you that if you are hesitant to mention any names which you would rather not state in public, you can ask for private session. Mr. Bakrac, will you be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac, Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. I already hereby inform you that it will be only very brief, that means not more than five to eight minutes that you will be in this courtroom today and that we'll continue on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Bakrac, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, before I put my question, can we call up P51. This is his witness statement. Witness, do you recall that in March and April of 2003 you gave a statement in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at pages 2 and 3 of the B/C/S version; namely, paragraph 6 entitled "Service in the MUP of Serbia." In this paragraph you said that in April of 1990, you were assigned to the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia and specifically in the police brigade there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The police brigade fell within the purview of public security, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Next you said that in 1991 you were assigned to the special units of the police. When exactly were these units set up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at this time when this was exactly. I believe it was in the month of July 1991, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As soon as the Special Police Units were set up, you became a member of one of them, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to the 1st Company of the 3rd Battalion, composed of predominantly members of Serb ethnicity who had come and joined the units in Belgrade from the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This Special Police Unit, and the term I'm using in the B/C/S is "milicija" deliberately because you will be aware that at a certain point thereafter it became a special unit of "policija," and please make sure that you make a pause before answering my question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Special Police Unit, as soon as it was formed, you became its member, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some 15 to 30 days after it was set up, as soon as decisions were taken as to who would be assigned where, so it wasn't right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This special unit of "milicija," was it formed so as to include a combat element?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a unit in my formation which had mortars, then for the most part we had light machine-guns, rifles, and we had four anti-tank vehicles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's be clear, this unit was envisaged as a unit which would take part in combat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since most of the men were policemen who had come over from the MUP in Croatia, the unit was designed to act for the most part as a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be precise. From the moment it was set up and throughout its existence, this special unit of "milicija" initially and later on of "policija" was always within the purview of the public security branch of the MUP of Serbia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of the police, but when we went out in the field, at least to the extent I was informed from the commander of my unit, we received orders and the rest from the state security sector. Now, what the prevailing practice was is not something I was privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We will come to the issue of who you received orders from. I am interested in what the case was formally and legally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, formally and legally it was part of public security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm looking at the clock and I see that we are past quarter to 2.00, could you wind up or is this a suitable moment to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The commander of this unit, the Special Police Unit or PJP, from the very beginning and then onwards as well, was it Obrad Stevanovic? Was Obrad Stevanovic the commander who was otherwise an employee in the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police brigade commander at the time was Mr. Stojan Petkovic, and the police brigade was composed of, well, a number of battalions. I don't want to stipulate the commanders of the battalions and units, but direct orders on the battle-field we received from the late Radovan Stojic, Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this opens up scope for further questions which I don't have time for, so I'd like to end there for today with your permission continuing on Wednesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Witness, before we adjourn I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given or still to be given. We are unable to sit in the early days of next week, that means that we'll only continue Wednesday quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. That may be inconvenient for you, we apologise for that, but there's no alternative. We will adjourn and we resume on Wednesday, the 1st of September, quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II.
